e.t: “Sinai” is the name of a mountain or region associated with Israel’s journey and worship of God. It is a place-name rather than a general description or action word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears 35 times, especially in Exodus, Numbers, and Leviticus. Scripture connects Sinai with Israel’s arrival, God’s presence, spoken commands, and the giving of the covenant testimony. The name therefore identifies a significant location where God addressed and instructed his people.

The surrounding verse context is needed to distinguish which individual is meant in each occurrence.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “truth.” It is a noun that names what is true and can describe the quality expected in speech, conduct, or a person. In the Old Testament, it is used in statements about speaking truth and living in truth. It occurs 127 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that truth is a broad and recurring scriptural concern.

e.t: This Hebrew verb means “delighted,” expressing pleasure or enjoyment. It describes someone taking pleasure in something rather than merely noticing or possessing it. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Nehemiah 9:25, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its role is verbal: it describes an action or state of delight connected with what is being discussed. This is the word’s basic lexical sense within its Hebrew biblical usage.

This Hebrew word refers to something presented before God for his attention and judgment, but its precise English meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Lamentations 3:59. In that passage, it functions as the object associated with God seeing and judging, so the surrounding verse is necessary to identify the exact matter being described.

Atarah is a Hebrew personal name, rendered as “Atarah.” It functions as a name rather than an ordinary descriptive word, so the available information identifies the person by name without giving a separate definition. In the Hebrew Bible, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 2:26. The reference establishes where the name appears, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain that occurrence’s particular context.

This word describes a sluggard—a person marked by unwillingness to apply himself to needed work. It functions as a noun referring to such a person, especially in the wisdom teaching of Proverbs. The word appears 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Proverbs, where it repeatedly identifies a settled pattern of laziness rather than a momentary delay or tiredness. Its meaning is therefore a person who persistently avoids diligence and responsibility. [p03:word:hebrew:H6102:renderings] [p03:word:hebrew:H6102:occurrences]

This Hebrew word means “barns,” referring to places where grain and other produce are kept. It is a noun used for storage buildings rather than for the produce itself. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 28:8 and Proverbs 3:10. In both passages, its basic sense concerns the storehouse or barn as the place connected with agricultural increase and provision.

Ether is a Hebrew place name, rendered “Ether.” It refers to a location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Joshua: once at Joshua 15:42 and again at Joshua 19:7. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific geographic setting cannot be explained here, but its lexical use is consistent: it identifies the place called Ether.

This Hebrew word means “edges.” It functions as a noun, referring to the edges of something rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in Judges 3:16. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context; the word itself identifies edges as the thing being mentioned.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “rivers,” describing flowing channels of water. It is used for waters that nourish, refresh, or spread outward, and it can appear in both literal descriptions and poetic pictures. The word occurs 10 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages that speak of water flowing beside trees, through a city, or from a place of abundance. Its surrounding wording determines the particular picture, but the central idea remains a river or watercourse carrying a continuing flow.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Paseah.” It identifies people rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs four times in the Old Testament, appearing in 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Its recorded uses are connected with genealogical or family listings and with people associated with Jerusalem’s rebuilding work. Thus, its ordinary meaning in these passages is the name Paseah; the surrounding verse is needed to identify which person bearing the name is intended.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “shield,” referring to protective equipment carried or used by warriors. It appears in descriptions of armed men, military forces, and royal weaponry, showing its normal connection with defense and battle. The word occurs 22 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 20 verses. It can describe a shield possessed by an individual or supplied as part of an army’s equipment. Its use in Ezekiel also places the shield among the weapons given to invading forces.

This Hebrew word refers to “watching,” describing the act or practice of keeping watch. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Lamentations 4:17. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its precise force in that occurrence cannot be expanded beyond this basic meaning. Its sense is therefore best understood as a reference to watching itself, rather than as a broader doctrine or theme.

This Hebrew word expresses the action “burn.” It functions as a verbal expression for something burning or being set alight. It occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its uses are connected with fire and its effects, including language describing what fire does. The surrounding verse determines what is burning and how the action is presented, but the word’s central sense remains the action of burning.

e.t: This word refers to "Keilah," a named place in the Old Testament. It functions as a place-name rather than as a description of an action, quality, or person. The name appears 18 times in the Hebrew Bible, with most occurrences in the account involving David and Keilah. It is also mentioned in Joshua, First Chronicles, and Nehemiah, showing its use as a continuing geographical name across Israel’s history.

This Hebrew verb means “read”: it describes the act of reading words or a message aloud or with understanding. In its Old Testament use, it appears 11 times, especially in Ezra and Daniel, where people read an official document, a decree, or writing. The word focuses on taking in and expressing what has been written, rather than on composing the message or explaining its meaning. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word describes something that “runneth”—that is, something flowing or running rather than remaining still. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew text, both times in Psalms: Psalm 23:5 and Psalm 66:12. Its use points to an overflowing condition or movement, but the precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. As a word connected with what runs, it functions in a sentence to describe or identify that flowing condition.

This Hebrew word means “trusted,” describing someone or something viewed in relation to trust. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Daniel 3:28, so its normal lexical range is represented by a single recorded use. The word points to trust as a stated description. Its precise force in Daniel 3:28 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.t: Abner is a Hebrew personal name, referring to the man named Abner rather than describing a general quality or action. In the Old Testament, it appears 63 times and is rendered “Abner.” The word functions as a name in narrative passages, especially in Samuel, where people speak about or address this individual. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical role is simply the person’s name.

This Hebrew word means “gathered,” describing the act of bringing things together. It functions as a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in Genesis. In each occurrence, it serves as the action word describing something being gathered. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence and the people or things being discussed.

Rephael is a Hebrew personal name, used to identify an individual rather than to describe an action, object, or quality. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 26:7, and is rendered “Rephael.” Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself provides identification but does not establish additional details about the person or the passage. Its meaning here is therefore best treated as the individual’s proper name.

e.t: This word means “Shuhite.” It identifies a person by a group or place designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew text of Job, it is used five times, each time in reference to the same designation. The word appears in passages involving Job’s companions and their speech, including their coming to him and addressing him. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its normal function is to identify someone as a Shuhite.

Arza is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Kings 16:9. As a name, its meaning is tied to the person it identifies, while the surrounding verse supplies the details of that person’s role. The English rendering is “Arza,” and no broader lexical definition is established here.

In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 21 times across 20 verses, including passages in Exodus, Ruth, Kings, Psalms, Jeremiah, and Hosea. Its basic meaning centers on people connected by proximity or residence, while the surrounding verse determines the particular relationship or situation being described.

The word appears in passages rendered with ideas of fear, storm, and overwhelming movement, but no single English phrase covers every occurrence.

Its exact force in each passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic role is to state what something is or how it stands.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “continual.” It describes something that continues as an ongoing practice, condition, or provision rather than occurring only once. In the Old Testament, it is used for regularly maintained worship, offerings, service, seeking God, and provisions given over time. The word occurs 104 times in the Hebrew Bible, showing a broad emphasis on persistence and ongoing duration.

This Hebrew word refers to a “stink,” identifying an offensive or foul smell. It occurs three times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, and each recorded rendering uses “stink.” The word appears in Isaiah 34:3, Joel 2:20, and Amos 4:10. In Amos 4:10, it functions as the object associated with several actions, showing that it can identify the resulting unpleasant odor. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word names a condition of “void”: it describes a place or state lacking established order or contents. It occurs three times in the Old Testament, in Genesis, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its repeated use shows a descriptive term for a stark, unformed condition rather than an action or person. The surrounding verse determines how that condition functions in each passage.

This Hebrew word means “among” or “between.” It marks the position or relation of one person, thing, or group in relation to others, showing that something is located within a group or separates two sides. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in two verses in Daniel 7:5 and 7:8. The exact force in any sentence depends on what the word connects, but its basic idea is a position among others or between distinct parties.
